o: We need to count integers x that divide both a and b. Any common factor of a and b must divide gcd(a, b), so the answer equals the number of divisors of gcd(a, b). For example 1, gcd(12, 6) = 6 and its divisors are 1, 2, 3, 6 → 4. For example 2, gcd(25, 30) = 5 with divisors 1, 5 → 2. Since a, b ≤ 1000, gcd(a, b) ≤ 1000, so even a brute-force scan up to min(a, b) is trivially fast; the constraints allow any divisor-counting method.
k: Every common factor of a and b is exactly a divisor of gcd(a, b), so counting common factors reduces to counting divisors of one number.
Divisors come in pairs (d, n/d), so you only need to iterate d up to sqrt(n) to count all divisors.
With a, b ≤ 1000, brute force over all candidates up to min(a, b) is perfectly acceptable.

a.i: Simply test every integer from 1 to min(a, b); if it divides both a and b, it is a common factor. This directly mirrors the definition and needs no number theory. With values at most 1000 it runs in microseconds.
s: Loop x from 1 to min(a, b).
If a % x == 0 and b % x == 0, increment the counter.
a.t: O(min(a, b)) — we check every candidate up to the smaller input.
a.sp: O(1) — only a counter is used.

a.i: By the properties of divisibility, x divides both a and b iff x divides g = gcd(a, b). So compute g via the Euclidean algorithm, then count divisors of g by iterating d from 1 to sqrt(g): each valid d contributes two divisors (d and g/d), taking care not to double-count when d*d == g.
s: Compute g = gcd(a, b) using the Euclidean algorithm.
For each d from 1 while d*d <= g: if g % d == 0, add 2 if d*d < g else add 1.
a.t: O(log(min(a, b)) + sqrt(gcd(a, b))) — Euclidean algorithm plus scanning up to sqrt(g).
a.sp: O(1) — constant extra space (recursion depth for gcd is logarithmic but negligible).

w: In an interview, mention the brute force first (it's correct and fast enough here), then present the GCD + sqrt approach as the optimal solution — it shows understanding that common factors are exactly divisors of gcd(a, b). Pitfalls: forgetting the perfect-square case when pairing divisors (d*d == g counts once, not twice), and using int overflow in C++/Java for d*d on larger inputs (cast to long). Edge cases: a == b (answer is the full divisor count of a), a or b equal to 1 (answer is always 1). Follow-ups might ask for the count of common multiples, or handling very large numbers where you'd need Pollard's rho for factoring.
